title: Delta County well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Delta County wells are typically about 90 ft deep with a 15 gpm median yield. See what that means for drilling cost, water level, and risk in this area.
h1: Water wells and drilling in Delta County, Colorado
intro_html:
Delta County has thousands of wells on record, from shallow alluvial holes along the rivers to deeper fractured-bedrock wells up on the benches. Looking at the county-wide data gives you a good starting point on how deep a new well might go, what kind of yield to expect, and what it typically costs to complete one here.

These numbers cover all permitted wells in the county, including areas around Delta, Cedaredge, Paonia, Hotchkiss, Orchard City, Crawford, and Lazear. Always pair this with a look at the specific well permits right around the parcel you’re buying or building on.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Delta County
sections.html:
Across Delta County, the median well depth is about 90 feet, with the middle half running from roughly 45 to 150 feet. That tells you a lot of domestic wells hit water fairly shallow, especially in alluvial and softer sedimentary areas.

About 54% of wells are under 100 feet, and another 40% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only 4% are in the 300–600 foot range and 1% go beyond 600 feet, even though the deepest well on record reaches 3,491 feet. For a driller’s bid, most parcels here will be quoted assuming something around that 90-foot range but with clear language on per-foot charges in case you land in one of the deeper fractured-bedrock pockets.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you usually get
sections.html:
Yields in Delta County are generally favorable. The reported median pump yield is 15 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10 and 15 gpm. That’s plenty for a typical exempt household well plus some outdoor use, assuming you stay within your permit terms.

About 55% of wells report more than 15 gpm, and 35% are in the 5–15 gpm band. Only 10% fall in the 1–5 gpm range, and there are no reported wells under 1 gpm in the yield data set. So low-yield or marginal wells do exist, but they show up in a small minority of reports. When you review nearby permits around Delta, Cedaredge, or Paonia, pay close attention to the listed test rate, not just depth.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they’re doing over time
sections.html:
Where it’s been measured, Delta County’s median static water level is about 25 feet below ground, with the middle half ranging from roughly 9 to 72 feet. That’s a fairly shallow water table in many spots, which is why so many wells are less than 150 feet deep.

The decade data suggests things are trending deeper: median depth to water was about 10 feet in the 2000s, 15 feet in the 2010s, and 36 feet so far in the 2020s. That points to a general decline in water levels in the wells that have been re-measured. Before buying, compare the older and newer static levels on nearby wells to see if your immediate area follows that same downward pattern or is more stable.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and how the pattern has changed
sections.html:
Delta County has 3,887 wells in the state records, with 2,264 marked as constructed and 2,371 listing a total depth. Most are in unnamed fractured-bedrock or similar aquifers, with a small number completed in the Mesa Verde Group and Mancos formations. There are no Denver Basin wells here.

Well permitting really picked up in the 1970s and 1990s, with 336 and 633 permits respectively. The 2000s were the busiest decade at 1,205 permits, followed by 444 in the 2010s and 306 already in the 2020s, with permits recorded through 2025. The work is concentrated among a few drillers: Bill Kissner Drilling Inc has 576 wells on record, Wildcat Drilling & Pump, Inc. 524, and K. W. Anderson Drilling 218. That history gives you a good paper trail to study around any parcel.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Delta County
sections.html:
In this county’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, typical drilling runs about $50–$75 per foot. At the county’s 90-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole itself roughly in the $4,500–$6,800 range before any equipment.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well at that median depth often lands around $10,500–$18,800. If you’re in an area where nearby wells are closer to 150–200 feet, adjust your budget upward using the same per-foot range. When you request bids, give the driller permit numbers for neighboring holes so they can quote more accurately instead of just using county-wide medians.

sections.heading: Local risks: contamination, low yield, and siting issues
sections.html:
Delta County’s records show generally strong yields, with no documented wells under 1 gpm in the reported data, so true “dry holes” are less common but still possible, especially in fractured bedrock away from valley fill. The bigger concern in some parts of the county is water quality.

Within about 10 miles, there are 31 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 62 historic mine features, and 12 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those don’t automatically mean a problem on your land, but it’s a strong argument for lab testing a new or existing well. Also factor in setbacks from septic systems and buildings when you lay out a homesite around Delta, Hotchkiss, Crawford, or Orchard City so you stay compliant and protect both the well and the leach field.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well in Delta County
sections.html:
Delta County’s well mix is mostly domestic and household use at about 68%, plus stock and irrigation wells scattered around the farms and benches. That tells you the area is generally workable for homes on wells, but you still want to do your homework parcel by parcel.

For any lot, pull the nearby permits and look at three things: depth, yield, and static water level trend. Compare a 1990s or 2000s well to more recent 2010s–2020s wells to see if the water table is dropping locally. If you’re buying an existing home, ask for recent well performance and any water-quality tests, especially near known PFAS or mining features. For raw land, tie your offer and build budget to a realistic well depth and the finished cost range shown by the county data.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Delta County, Colorado?
faq.a: County-wide, the median well depth is about 90 feet, with the middle half of wells between roughly 45 and 150 feet. Around 54% of wells are under 100 feet deep and 40% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only a small share extend deeper than 300 feet, even though one recorded well reaches 3,491 feet. Always check depths on nearby permits around your specific parcel for a better local estimate.

faq.q: How much water do wells in Delta County usually produce?
faq.a: Reported yields are strong overall. The median pump rate is about 15 gallons per minute, with the middle half of wells between 10 and 15 gpm. Roughly 55% of wells report more than 15 gpm and 35% fall in the 5–15 gpm range. Only about 10% are down in the 1–5 gpm band, and none of the reported wells show yields below 1 gpm in the dataset.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Delta County?
faq.a: Static water level data suggests a downward trend in the wells that have been measured. Median depth to water was around 10 feet in the 2000s, 15 feet in the 2010s, and about 36 feet so far in the 2020s. The overall median static level across records is about 25 feet, with a wide spread from roughly 9 to 72 feet. Check nearby wells by decade to see if your immediate area shows the same pattern.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Delta County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Delta County’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, typical drilling rates run about $50–$75 per foot. At the county’s 90-foot median depth, that puts the borehole in the neighborhood of $4,500–$6,800. A complete domestic well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually ends up around $10,500–$18,800 at that depth. Deeper local wells will scale up from there using the same per-foot rate.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Delta County?
faq.a: The permit records don’t rate water quality, but they do show potential risk sources: about 31 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 62 historic mine features, and 12 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles. Many private wells are fine, but safety depends on your exact location. Before relying on any well for drinking, have it tested by a certified lab for basic potability and any contaminants of concern in your area.
